open-question.question: The tool needs a partial strip that clears only the recommendation, depends-on, and applied-principle children while keeping the alternatives, and the full strip that clears every child still serves as the hatch for a stale alternative set. Is the partial strip a flag on the existing strip subcommand, a new subcommand, or the new default of strip with the full strip behind a flag?
open-question.alternative: Keep `strip`'s bare form clearing every child and add a mode flag — `strip --recommendation SHORT_TITLE…` — that clears only the `<recommendation>`, `<depends-on>` and `<applied-principle>` children and leaves the `<alternative>` set standing, the same narrowing the cascade applies internally through the one shared per-block primitive. It follows the polarity this tool already establishes, where the bare subcommand is the broad uniform treatment and a flag narrows it — `remove` bare strips every dependent and `--option` narrows, `list` bare prints every block and `--unannotated` narrows — so nothing shipped changes meaning: every existing `strip` call, `test_strip.py`'s pinned strip-to-bare outcome, and every sentence saying strip clears every child stay true and unedited, and `strip --recommendation` reads as the exact mirror of an `embed` that names the same half with the same word. The hatch the new design makes routine — clear a stale recommendation so the inline pass can re-run it — is the longer form, while the rarer and more expensive one is a bare word, so a mistyped `strip` discards an alternative set that cost a parallel agent dispatch.

Invert the subcommand: bare `strip` clears only the recommendation, depends-on and applied-principle children, and the full clear moves behind a flag such as `strip --all`. The bare word does the safe, now-routine thing and the one operation that throws away parallel-dispatch work must be asked for explicitly, so the expensive artifact is guarded by the command form itself rather than by the caller having read the right hatch sentence. It silently redefines a shipped subcommand — same command, no error, different result — so an old chain or a user's muscle memory quietly stops clearing what it cleared, and every `strip` sentence in CLAUDE.md, `docs/`, and the sweep's hatch plus `test_strip.py`'s pinned semantics must be re-pointed in one change, against the tool's own bare-is-broad polarity.

Leave `strip` untouched and add a second verb for the partial clear (for example `unrecommend SHORT_TITLE…`), both implemented over one shared per-block primitive. Each verb carries exactly one meaning and one argparse help text end to end, no flag can be omitted or mistyped, and `strip`'s existing contract, tests, and every sentence describing it stand entirely unchanged. It puts two names in front of one write whose only difference is which child kinds survive — precisely the case this tool spells as a mode flag everywhere else — adding an eleventh verb, its own test file, and a naming question of its own, and reading inconsistently beside an `embed` whose two shapes are named by flags.
open-question.recommendation: Two blast radii for one write is what this tool spells as a flag on the broad bare form, exactly as `remove --option` narrows `remove`, and keeping the full strip as the default leaves every shipped call, test, and sentence about `strip` true while the new flag reads as the mirror of embed's recommendation shape; only if a bare `strip` slip were unrecoverable, rather than one re-dispatch of the alternatives pass, would flipping the default win instead.

open-question.question: The inline recommendation pass reasons over the whole question set at once but must still write each block with one embed call, and embed resolves every depends-on tag against a sibling that already carries a recommendation. Does the skill order its embed calls so every declared target is written before its dependents, or does the tool relax the one-hop check for this pass?
open-question.alternative: Leave the tool's one-hop check exactly as it is and make the inline skill sequence its per-block `embed --recommendation` calls so every block it declares a tag on is written before its dependents, resolving any mutual declaration itself before the first write. Not one line of the tool changes — `check_dependencies`, its two refusal strings and `test_embed.py`'s pins all stand — and the property that every embedded tag names a sibling already carrying a `<recommendation>` keeps holding at every intermediate state, so a run interrupted halfway leaves a document whose every tag resolves exactly as `walk` expects. It puts a topological ordering rule back into skill prose, which is precisely what the answer sweep moved into the tool's `walk` (those rules live in the tool and `tests/test_walk.py`, and the skill states none of them), and it is the one option under which a genuine mutual dependency — newly expressible now that a single runner decides every block at once — has no valid write order at all, so the skill must carry a cycle-breaking rule the tool deliberately refuses to have.

Drop the target-carries-a-`<recommendation>` half of the `<depends-on>` resolution and keep the other: a tag must name another block of the document that carries `<alternative>` children, and its option must be one of that block's own alternative ids — so the recommendation pass may write its blocks in any order and states no ordering rule at all. The dropped half is the one predicate the two-pass split makes meaningless — it encoded that the agent read that sibling's already-embedded recommendation, which the inline pass abolishes by holding every recommendation at once — while the half that does the real work stays fully enforceable, because the pass stops unless every block already carries its frozen alternatives; and since the recommendation shape is the only fragment shape carrying `<depends-on>`, this is one uniform rule rather than a pass-scoped exception, leaving the tool with one condition fewer rather than one mode more. A tag may now be written naming a sibling the run never gets a recommendation onto (a block skipped or refused mid-run), so the document can hold a tag whose target carries none — a state `walk` already absorbs by dropping the edge and `remove --option` by keying only on the recorded option, but one the embed check used to make unreachable.

Retire the per-block write for this pass: the skill pipes one fragment covering every block in a single `embed` call, validated and written atomically, so there is no call ordering and no partially-annotated intermediate document. Ordering, cycles and intermediate states all stop being questions at once, and one write matches the pass's whole-set reasoning and its single per-run commit exactly. It needs a second fragment format carrying the wrapper lines every current shape check refuses outright, with its own per-block anchors, preconditions and refusal strings, and it makes one bad block refuse the whole run's reasoning where a per-block call refuses one block and leaves the rest embedded.
open-question.recommendation: The check's recommendation half records a sequential-dispatch fact the inline pass abolishes, while the half that keeps a tag meaningful stays enforceable against the frozen alternatives every block must already carry, so dropping it removes a condition from the tool instead of adding a graph-ordering rule to prose the answer sweep deliberately emptied of one; only if a tag naming a recommendation-less sibling were worse than the edge `walk` already drops would ordering the embed calls win instead.

open-question.question: The current sweep judges every agent return by last-line verdict, then embed, then exactly one repair (a same-session continuation where the host can continue one, otherwise one fresh re-dispatch). Does the parallel alternatives pass keep that whole pipeline per return, with the shape reminder rewritten for an alternatives-only fragment whose anchors are the first <alternative line and the last </alternative> line?
open-question.alternative: The alternatives pass runs the same three-stage per-return pipeline the sweep runs today, on each return as it lands: the last-non-whitespace-line `FAILED:` verdict (skipped, never repaired), then the whole message piped to `embed --alternatives`, then exactly one repair on a refusal — a same-session continuation where the host can continue a finished agent session, one fresh re-dispatch where it cannot — with the fixed one-slot corrective template rewritten for the alternatives-only fragment, asking for the `<alternative>` elements with their `<advantage>` and `<drawback>` children as the whole final message and quoting the two shape tests that now bound it: first non-whitespace text starting `<alternative`, last non-whitespace text ending `</alternative>`. Nothing the split changed weakens the case that produced this pipeline, and one thing it changed strengthens it — because the recommendation pass stops while any question lacks alternatives, an unrepaired skip no longer leaves one thin block among annotated siblings but holds up the whole downstream pass until a re-run, so the cheap recovery a same-session continuation buys, where the agent re-emits from grounding it has already paid for, is worth most exactly where a wide fan-out made that grounding most expensive; and the only piece the pass has to restate is the template, whose single slot, two branches and one-attempt budget all carry over unchanged. It carries the whole repair apparatus — two host-keyed branches, a rendered template, a spent-or-unspent budget per question — into a pass whose returns arrive concurrently, so the runner holds a live handle and a budget for many questions at once instead of one at a time, and it keeps a long prose stage for a failure the tool's own slice has already made rare.

Drop the repair stage from this pass: read the last-line verdict, pipe the whole message to `embed --alternatives`, and treat any refusal as an immediate per-question skip noted in the end-of-run advisory with the tool's `Error:` line, recovery being a bare re-run that the alternatives filter narrows to exactly the skipped questions. It is the shortest pipeline that still cannot let prose reach the document, it holds no per-question state across concurrent returns, and it rests on a real change rather than a preference: the failure that motivated the repair — well-formed elements under a grounding summary — is now absorbed by the tool's slice instead of refused, so what is left for a repair to fix is the rarer genuinely malformed fragment, against which a filtered re-run is a comparable remedy. It restores exactly the skip-only behaviour this repository records as already reversed once and marks as not to be restored, and it pays for one malformed return with a second whole pass whose every dispatch re-grounds, while the recommendation pass stays stopped until that re-run lands.

Keep the repair but collapse its two branches to the one every host supports: on a refusal, dispatch one fresh alternatives agent for that question with the same prompt plus the rewritten shape reminder, never a continuation of the finished session. One repair behaviour then holds on every host, so the dispatch step carries a single capability branch — the one for fan-out width — rather than two, and no agent handle has to survive across a wide concurrent fan-out for a repair that may never be spent. Every repair re-pays the entire grounding cost the pass just spent, making the branch the current sweep names explicitly as the fallback into the only path, which is the most expensive possible answer to a formatting slip, and it retires the plugin's one worked use of session continuation.

Keep all three stages but send no rendered reminder: the repair message is the tool's `Error: <reason>` line alone, on the premise that the agent's own step 4 already states the shape tests and still holds them in context on the continuation branch. The two anchors then live in exactly one runtime file — the agent's self-check — so the pass can never drift from it, sparing this pass the duplication cost the shape flag already pays at its call sites. On the fresh-re-dispatch branch the new agent receives an error about a message it never sent and no statement of the shape to hit, which is close to the blind attempt the template was introduced to replace, and even on the continuation branch it withholds the one restatement that helps when the first self-check passed on a wrong reading.
open-question.recommendation: The pipeline is this repository's one worked answer to a malformed return, and the split gives it more to do rather than less — an unrepaired skip now holds up the recommendation pass, not merely its own block — so only the template changes, rewritten around the anchors the alternatives shape introduced; only if a repaired alternatives return proved no likelier to embed than a plain filtered re-run would dropping the repair win instead.

open-question.question: The parallel alternatives pass needs the ids of the blocks that carry no alternative elements, which the existing list --unannotated (no recommendation element) does not express. What is the new list filter called, and does --unannotated keep its current meaning?
open-question.alternative: Retire the `--unannotated` spelling and give `list` two symmetric negative filters named for the child kind each tests — `--without-alternatives` (the parallel pass's dispatch set, and the inline pass's one-call stop test) and `--without-recommendation`, which carries today's semantics unchanged as the recommendation pass's idempotency skip. Each flag states the element it tests, so neither pass's set has to be remembered from a convention, and the same two words name the same two halves across every surface this milestone touches — `embed --alternatives` / `--recommendation` and `strip --recommendation` — while the `without-` prefix keeps a filter's negative polarity explicit where a bare `--alternatives` would read as the blocks that have them; the split is precisely what costs `--unannotated` its single referent, since a block carrying alternatives is annotated yet that filter would still print it. It renames a shipped flag, so the sweep skill, `docs/skill-reference.md`, the two CLAUDE.md entries and the five test files that spell `--unannotated` (`test_list.py`, `test_sort.py`, `test_walk.py`, `test_embed.py`, `test_strip.py`) must be re-pointed in the same change, and the tool's most-called read becomes the wordiest line in both passes.

Leave `--unannotated` exactly as it is — spelling and meaning — and add one new flag beside it for the other half, for example `list --without-alternatives`, so nothing shipped changes. It is strictly additive: every existing call, pinned test assertion and sentence about `--unannotated` stays true and unedited, the recommendation pass keeps the gather line it already runs, and the whole tool diff is one argparse flag, one `cmd_list` branch and one test. The two set-defining filters then rest on different naming principles — one on the element it tests, one on a word the split has just left with two possible referents — so every reader of either skill must carry the convention that annotated means the recommendation half alone, and a later child kind arrives with no pattern to follow.

Give `--unannotated` the new meaning — blocks carrying no `<alternative>`, the wholly bare block the first pass targets — and move today's meaning to a second new flag such as `--unrecommended`. The plainest word then literally names the block with nothing embedded and points at the pipeline's new front, so the filter a user meets first is the one spelled most simply. It is exactly the silent redefinition the sibling `strip` question rejected — same flag, no error, a different set — so every sentence and pinned test naming `--unannotated` is quietly false until re-pointed, it pays for two renames rather than one, and it leaves a pair whose two words differ only by a suffix.

Replace `--unannotated` with one filter that takes the child kind as its value — `list --missing alternatives` and `list --missing recommendation` — over an argparse `choices` list. One flag covers both halves and any later child kind with no further naming question, and because its value is the element name itself the filter can never be read in the wrong polarity. It makes `list` the first read filter with a required value, so a bare `--missing` is an argparse usage error rather than a meaningful call, and it buys extensibility for a format whose two annotation halves this very milestone freezes.
open-question.recommendation: Today's filter keeps its exact meaning and its job as the recommendation pass's idempotency skip but not its spelling, because the split leaves annotated with two referents — a block carrying alternatives is annotated, yet `--unannotated` would still print it — so each filter is named for the element it tests, which also keeps one pair of words meaning one pair of halves across `list`, `embed` and `strip`; only if this flag were typed by users outside this repository, rather than only by the two passes and the test suite, would the additive option's zero churn win instead.

open-question.question: The inline recommendation pass reasons over the whole question set at once. On a re-run where some blocks already carry a recommendation, does it leave those untouched and recommend only on the blocks lacking one, as today's --unannotated idempotency does, or may it revise an existing recommendation in light of the whole set?
open-question.alternative: The inline pass gathers the blocks carrying no recommendation, reasons over the whole document but writes only those, and reads every surviving recommendation as context it may declare a dependency on — revision is the explicit hatch, a partial strip on the named blocks followed by a re-run, exactly as today's idempotency skip works. It is the set the narrowed cascade already computes: an answer clears the recommendation half of precisely the blocks whose reasoning it invalidated and leaves the rest standing, so "lacks a recommendation" is the cascade's own verdict about what must be re-derived rather than a second guess at it, and the tool enforces the rule at the write — the recommendation shape refuses a block that already carries one — so idempotency stays a filter plus a precondition with no prose inspection of blocks the pass is not writing, and the hatch is now cheap and precise because the partial strip clears the pick while leaving the parallel pass's expensive alternatives untouched. The pass's whole-set coherence then holds only over the subset it writes: a newly surfaced question that ought to change several standing recommendations can do no more than note the tension in its own rationale, and because the frozen blocks are never rewritten they can never gain a depends-on naming that new question, so the dependency graph only ever grows forward and a user who wants the older picks reconsidered must know to strip them first.

Every run clears the recommendation half of every block itself and re-embeds all of them, so each run leaves one globally consistent recommendation set derived in a single act of whole-set reasoning. The coherence claim that motivates the inline pass holds unconditionally over the entire document rather than over whatever subset happened to be empty, no stale pick can survive a re-run, the dependency graph is rebuilt in full so an older block can declare on a newly added origin question, and there is one rule with no filter, no hatch and nothing the user must know to invoke. It abolishes idempotency: a re-run rewrites recommendations the user has already read and may be part-way through answering one by one, churns the diff and the single run commit body with blocks whose substance did not change, and makes the narrowed cascade pointless — its careful agreeing-versus-disagreeing discrimination is erased by a pass that rewrites the agreeing dependents anyway, which is the one thing the whole cascade change was made to avoid.

The pass writes every block lacking a recommendation and additionally strips and re-embeds any standing recommendation its whole-set view judges contradicted, printing an advisory naming each block it revised. It buys the coherence of blanket re-recommendation at a fraction of the churn, rewriting only the picks the new whole-set view actually contradicts — the very case the skip option can address only with a prose note in someone else's rationale. Idempotency becomes a judgment rather than a filter, so two consecutive runs over an unchanged document can differ and a recommendation the user is about to answer can vanish under an unrelated re-run; it requires the pass to inspect and rule on blocks it is not writing, which is exactly the prose inspection the sweep's idempotency rule keeps out; and each silent overwrite needs its own advisory because the diff alone cannot say why a settled pick moved.
open-question.recommendation: The narrowed cascade already decides which blocks' reasoning an answer invalidated, so the recommendation-less set is the set to write and the rest is the set to trust, and the recommendation-shape precondition makes that a refusal in the tool rather than a discretion in prose — keeping idempotency a filter, keeping a pick the user is mid-answer on stable, and leaving revision to a partial strip that now costs only the pick and never the alternatives; only if the whole-set view routinely contradicted recommendations the cascade had deliberately left standing would re-recommending the whole set win instead.

open-question.question: Alternatives are frozen, but a sibling's recorded decision can make an embedded alternative infeasible before the recommendation pass runs. When the inline pass judges a block's alternative set stale or dead, does it skip that block and print an advisory naming the full strip as the remedy, recommend the best surviving option and note the dead one in the rationale, or stop the run?
open-question.alternative: The inline pass writes no recommendation for a block whose alternative set it judges stale, and prints those Short Titles with the reason alongside its terse line, naming the full strip plus a re-run of the alternatives pass as the remedy. No pick is ever derived from a premise the recorded decisions contradict, and the shape already exists — it is the sweep's still-skipped advisory verbatim, git-absent and decision-critical — with one block's problem never touching the recommendations the run writes for the rest. Nothing in the document records the verdict, so every later run re-gathers the block, re-judges it stale and re-skips it until the user acts, while the dead alternative stays embedded and liftable exactly as it would under any other option; and the remedy it names is the pipeline's most expensive one, discarding a whole parallel-dispatched alternative set even when one option of four died and the rest still stand.

The pass recommends the best still-viable alternative and states in the rationale which option the recorded decision killed and why, falling back to the skip-with-advisory above only for a block where no alternative survives at all. It fits the case the frozen-alternatives design actually produces — a sibling decision that kills one option, or only the premise of one drawback, while the others stand — so the run converges instead of leaving a block no run can ever finish, and the staleness verdict lands in the committed document and the run's commit body rather than in a console line git never keeps. The lift that records the answer prints the whole rationale, so the dead-option note is folded verbatim into the recorded decision prose, and the block keeps the dead <alternative> child where an alternative-derived answer can still lift it as a decision.

A stale set is treated as a precondition failure like a missing one: the pass names the block and stops before any write, pointing at the full strip and a re-run of both passes. One uniform input-not-fit-for-this-pass stop covers both faults, matching the stop the goal already gives the pass when any question lacks alternatives, and it leaves git untouched so no half-set of picks lands on a document the pass has judged inconsistent. It gives one block a veto over a whole run of whole-set reasoning, the blast radius a per-block write exists to avoid, and unlike the missing-alternatives stop that one list call decides, it rests on a judgment the user cannot check before the run refuses — so a set with several stale blocks converges only after as many stop-fix-rerun cycles.

The pass runs the full strip on the stale block itself, committing that clearing with the run, so the block reappears in the alternatives pass's dispatch set and is regenerated there. The document ends in a state that matches the verdict rather than carrying a set the pass has judged dead, so the block heals through the existing two-pass pipeline with nothing the user must know beyond re-running the first pass. The recommendation pass becomes a destructive writer of the half it only consumes, discarding parallel-dispatched work on its own unreviewed judgment with no record of what it discarded beyond the diff, and it leaves the document failing this pass's own start precondition, so the next recommendation run stops on the block it just cleared.
open-question.recommendation: The frozen set is meant to outlive decisions that outdate part of it, and the narrowed cascade keeps the alternatives precisely so an override costs only a re-run of the pick, so a pass that refuses to pick whenever it sees staleness hands back the cost that narrowing was made to remove — naming the best surviving option and why the other died is exactly the hedge-free single pick with a stated reason the analytical core already asks for, and keeping the skip as the floor for a set with nothing left means the expensive full strip is named only when it truly is the remedy; only if a recorded decision could not carry a clause saying which option the earlier answer killed would skipping every stale block win instead.

open-question.question: /discuss-open-question must work on a block in any state and reuse embedded alternatives when present. In that case may it surface an option the embedded set lacks, and how does it present the embedded recommendation when the block carries one: as its own starting recommendation to defend or challenge, or as context beside a fresh one?
open-question.alternative: On a block carrying alternatives, discuss reuses them as its option set rather than re-enumerating, and may put an option the set lacks on the table marked as a departure from the frozen set; it then runs the pick half itself and states one recommendation of its own, showing any embedded `<recommendation>` beside it as the sweep's standing pick and saying plainly whether the two agree and why. An independent second read is the one thing the conversation can add that the pass could not — a user who invokes discuss on an annotated block has by that act declined to simply accept the standing pick — and the agreement or disagreement between the two picks is the most decision-relevant signal the skill can produce, which a skill that only defends the standing pick structurally cannot generate; it also keeps discuss's composition over the split core uniform, reusing the enumeration half's output whenever alternatives are present and always running the pick half, rather than making that reference conditional on whether a `<recommendation>` happens to sit in the block. It puts two picks in front of a user who came for one decision, in tension with the skill's own "a concrete decision by the end of the conversation — not a design document" framing, and the fresh pick is formed without the inline pass's whole-set view, so it can differ merely because it saw less; and when the user takes a departure option, the recorded answer matches no `<alternative id>`, so the literal-answer path strips every dependent's pick instead of reconciling it by exact id.

Discuss reuses the embedded alternatives, and when the block carries a `<recommendation>` it adopts that as the position on the table — restating its rationale as the opening position and running the "what would change your mind" layer against it rather than forming a rival pick — while still allowing an option outside the set to be raised as a named departure. It starts the conversation where the document already stands, so the cheapest recording paths stay live end to end: agreement records through `/answer-open-question-with-recommendation`, a move to another embedded option through `/answer-open-question-with-alternative`, both exact-id and both leaving agreeing dependents' tags standing; and the conversation is spent testing one pick instead of re-deriving a pick the inline pass made with a whole-set view discuss cannot reconstruct. An embedded recommendation is batch-produced and, by this repository's own provenance rule, is never read as user-deliberated reasoning — so making it the opening position anchors the user on the weakest-warranted claim in the block at exactly the moment the skill exists for, a question the user could not answer outright — and because the recommendation pass never revises a standing pick, a pick the whole-set view has since outgrown gets defended rather than re-examined.

Discuss is confined to the embedded alternatives — it may not put an option outside them on the table, routing a genuinely missing option to the refresh path of a partial strip plus a re-run of the alternatives pass — and presents the embedded recommendation as the standing position to defend or challenge. Every decision coming out of discuss is then an embedded `<alternative id>`, so every answer it leads to records by exact id and the narrowed cascade's agreeing branch fires — no discuss-driven answer ever strips a dependent — and "frozen" means the same thing in every runner rather than holding for the passes and quietly lapsing in conversation. It gags the one human-in-the-loop skill at precisely the point where a missing option is most likely to surface, since the alternatives pass enumerates per question, in parallel, with no conversation; and the detour it prescribes — strip, re-run the parallel pass, re-read — costs far more than the literal answer it avoids, which under the narrowed cascade costs only a re-run of the pick.
open-question.recommendation: Discuss writes nothing, so the freeze it must honour is the alternative set the two passes own and not the pick sitting beside it — reusing the frozen options keeps the parallel pass's expensive work while forming its own recommendation adds the one thing the sweep cannot, an independent read whose agreement or disagreement with the standing pick is itself what a user who declined to just accept that pick came for, and which matters more because the recommendation pass will never revisit it; only if a discuss-formed pick routinely diverged from the inline pass's whole-set reasoning without being the better call would defending the standing pick win instead.

open-question.id: Recommendation run commit subject and body
open-question.question: The inline recommendation pass commits once per run with its reasoning in the commit body. What is the subject (for example Recommendation-annotation: <milestone_id>), and what shape does the body take: one line per question in the lifted option-and-rationale form, or free prose covering the whole set?
open-question.alternative: The pass commits once under `Recommendation-annotation: <milestone_id>` — today's marker with the whole-run descriptor every once-per-run committer here already carries — and its body is one `lift`-printed "`<option>` — `<rationale>`" line per question the run annotated, gathered after the embeds and before the sort. Every body line is the tool's own print of text the same commit added, so the body cannot drift from its diff — the property `Principle-capture:`'s composed one-line-per-change body is built to preserve and the one today's annotation body has by construction — while the marker, the line form and the per-question `lift` call all carry over unchanged from the sweep this pass replaces, so the split costs the commit convention one descriptor and nothing else; because the run writes only the recommendation-less blocks, the body is one line per block this run decided rather than a restatement of the whole document on every re-run, and a block the run judged stale carries its surviving-option verdict into the body for free, the body being exactly those rationales. It restates verbatim what the same commit's diff adds, at the run's full scale — a first pass over a set this size stacks fourteen rationales — and records only the per-block picks, so whatever whole-set reasoning became neither a rationale clause nor a `<depends-on>` element is kept nowhere; and the marker's readability rests on the still-open `Alternatives pass commit subject and body` taking the matching `Alternatives-annotation:` form, since a sibling marker outside that family would leave `Recommendation-annotation:` naming a half whose counterpart is unnamed.

Same subject, but the body is free prose the pass composes once for the run: how it read the set as a whole, which picks turned on which siblings, and what it did with any block it could not settle. It is the only shape that records the thing this pass exists to produce and the diff cannot show — the cross-question reasoning behind a set of picks made together, including the couplings weighed and rejected that never became an element — and it stays one short paragraph whatever the question count, where per-question lines grow with the set. It is composed text backed by no tool print, unique among the plugin's bodies (every other is a tool's own line, a heading, or the user's own words), so nothing pins it to the diff it describes and an over-long or hedged paragraph has no check; and it gives up the per-decision grep line every answer and annotation commit in the log carries today.

Same subject with a two-part body: a short composed paragraph on the whole-set reasoning and any block the run left unsettled, then the lifted line per annotated question beneath it. Each half records what only it can — the tool's lines for what the document now holds, one paragraph for the run-level reasoning and the skips a diff cannot show — and neither half is new to the repo, the lines being today's body and the paragraph the `Principle-capture:` body's composed-at-commit-time form. It is the plugin's first two-part commit body, so the skill must specify both halves and the boundary between them, and the paragraph's content is largely the union of clauses the lines below already carry — the composed half most likely to be written as a summary of the very lines it sits above, which is redundancy carrying the drift risk without either half's strength.

The body of the first option under a new marker naming what the pass now does — for instance `Recommendation-pick: <milestone_id>` — leaving `Recommendation-annotation:` to the pre-split commits that embedded a whole analysis at once. It keeps one marker meaning one payload across the whole history, which matters precisely here because the split changes what such a commit holds — a run's picks against frozen alternatives rather than one question's alternatives and pick together — and the commit convention derives markers from distinctive function with no grandfathered exceptions. It breaks the pairing the split's own vocabulary creates, two annotating passes whose markers differ in exactly the word naming their half, and it buys a distinction the descriptor already makes plain (a Short Title before the split, a milestone id after) at the price of one more prefix a log reader must learn and every doc surface must name.
open-question.recommendation: The pass writes a recommendation per block, so the record git keeps should be per block too, and the lifted line is that record already written and already printed by the tool rather than composed a second time as prose nothing pins to the diff; keeping `Recommendation-annotation:` names the half this pass owns beside its alternatives sibling, and swapping the descriptor to the milestone id is what every once-per-run committer here already does, so the split costs the commit convention one word; only if a run's whole-set reasoning routinely failed to fit inside the rationales that run produced would the lead paragraph be worth its drift risk.

open-question.id: Alternatives pass commit subject and body
open-question.question: /provide-alternatives-to-all-open-questions embeds and commits each return as it lands. What is its commit subject (for example Alternatives-annotation: <Short Title>), what if anything goes in the body given that lift prints only recommendation or single-alternative lines, and what is its one fixed terse success line?
open-question.alternative: Commit each embedded return under `Alternatives-annotation: <Short Title>` with no body at all — the subject-only form `commit-procedure.md` already provides for when a caller supplies no BODY — and report the run with the one fixed line `Alternatives embedded.`, the reporting invariant's own no-op line and still-skipped advisory being the only other output. It answers all three halves from conventions already in the repo and invents nothing: the marker is `Recommendation-annotation:`'s sibling differing in exactly the word that names its half, so the two passes read as the two halves of one annotation and the counterpart the recommendation sibling's drawback leaves unnamed is filled; the descriptor is the Short Title because the commit is per return, exactly as every per-item commit here carries its item's handle while every once-per-run one carries the milestone id; the body is omitted because this half has no one-line tool print to hold — `lift` prints a recommendation or a single named alternative and nothing else — and subject-only commits are ordinary here, `Question-ordering:` among them; and `Alternatives embedded.` is the existing success line with one noun changed, identifier-free as the rule requires. It also stays clear of capture's anchors by construction, since that grep is anchored and its `Alternative-answer` branch cannot match `Alternatives-annotation`. It leaves the one annotation family inconsistent in the log — the recommendation half carries its rationale in the body, this half carries nothing — so `git log` says which questions gained alternatives but never which alternatives, and reviewing a wide parallel run means opening one diff per commit; and the marker sits one letter from `Alternative-answer:`, so a human skim or a loosely written `Alternative-` grep can conflate an annotation with an answer.

Same subject and success line, but give each commit a body of one `lift --alternative "<id>"` line per embedded alternative — "`<id>` — `<what-it-is>`" — the ids recovered after the embed from a `locate` of the block the call just wrote. It holds the whole annotation family's bodies to the single rule the recommendation sibling's pick turns on — every body line is the tool's own print of text the same commit added, so a body cannot drift from its diff — and it puts each question's enumerated option ids in the log where a reviewer scanning a wide parallel run reads them without opening a diff. Nothing the pass already runs prints those ids, so the body costs a `locate` plus a prose read of the printed block to recover them and then one `lift` call per alternative, reintroducing into the busiest loop in the plugin exactly the orchestrator-side reading of a block's contents that this design has otherwise moved into the tool — and what it yields is an unbounded multi-line restatement of the very children the same commit's one-element-per-line canonical diff already shows.

Keep the subject and the success line and give the tool a whole-block alternatives print — for example `lift --alternatives "<Short Title>"`, one "`<id>` — `<what-it-is>`" line per alternative — so this half's body is one tool call, as the recommendation half's is. It recovers a tool-printed, drift-proof body in exactly one call per commit with no reading of the block by the pass at all, and the same print would serve any later consumer needing a block's option roster without a `locate`. It widens the tool — a new flag, its refusal strings and its own test coverage — beyond the three tool changes the goal names, and does so for a commit body alone, producing text that is a second copy of the diff it rides in, which is the thinnest reason in this repo to add a tool surface.

Derive the marker from the pass's own name rather than from the sweep it splits off — `Alternatives-provision: <Short Title>`, or `Alternatives-enumeration:` — with the body and the success line as in the first option. It derives the marker straight from the skill's distinctive function the way the commit convention asks of a new marker, and it puts a whole word between this marker and `Alternative-answer:`, so no log skim or hand-written grep can conflate the two. It breaks the pairing the split's own vocabulary creates — two annotating passes whose markers differ in exactly the word naming their half — leaving `Recommendation-annotation:` reading as a leftover rather than one of a pair, and it buys separation from an answer marker no automated reader can confuse, since capture's grep is both-ends-anchored and names its three branches literally.

depends-on.question: Recommendation run commit subject and body

open-question.recommendation: The split produces two annotating halves, so their markers should differ in exactly the word that names the half — `Alternatives-annotation: <Short Title>` per return beside `Recommendation-annotation: <milestone_id>` per run, the descriptor following the commit's granularity as it already does everywhere here — and the body is left empty because this half has no one-line tool print to put in it and every substitute is either a block read the tool was built to absorb or a restatement of the same commit's diff, while `Alternatives embedded.` is the existing success line with one noun changed; only if a reviewer routinely had to know a block's option ids from the log alone, without opening the diff, would adding the whole-block print be worth its tool surface.
